content:
As requested, this can be a discussion thread for the lean-zip library, and the associated blog post / LinkedIn post.

tl;dr: lean-zip is faster than the pure Rust implementation miniz_oxide at every compression level, and faster than zlib-rs (the careful-use-of-unsafe-internally Rust library) at compression level 9. How? Prove the theorem that the algorithm is correct, and then aggressively optimize using AIs.

(I'll note one extra caveat that isn't reflected in the blog post: there's some evidence now that I've over-optimized for the Silesia corpus. I'm working on fixing that now. If anyone knows of bigger/better standard corpora for testing compression algorithms, please let me know about them.)
Is there a short summary of how features like implemented_by are used for achieving performance gains?

One question : lean-zip has a proof that decompress ( compress data ) = data, but i guess there is also a proof that compress follows a proper spec of the compression algorithm.
So a natural question is how confident are you that this spec is correct ? is there any chance that claude gamed the spec to squeeze more performance out of it and achieve it's goal ?

A side question, i'm really interrested in using the lean part (not the ffi) of lean-zip to implement the Http compression algorithms for LeanIO and so another question would be: would you be willing to provide a lean only version of lean-zip without the ffi as i don't like the idea to add more dependencies than necessary to LeanIO
Once the Lean compiler can emit AVX512 instructions (hopefully in a somewhat formally verifiable way) we'd be unstoppable!

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Is there a short summary of how features like implemented_by are used for achieving performance gains?

We just use @[extern] for some low level things, like word-sized reads and writes out of ByteArray. (And BitVec.ctz, counting trailing zeroes in a bitvector.) I'm working on getting these into the Lean runtime. There's nothing specifically relevant for DEFLATE that is implemented in C.

Alfredo Moreira-Rosa said:

So a natural question is how confident are you that this spec is correct ? is there any chance that claude gamed the spec to squeeze more performance out of it and achieve it's goal ?

Moderately? Adversarial review is welcome. Note this project also relies on good-old-fashioned conformance testing, i.e. that we can decompress streams from other implementations, and they can decompress ours.

Alfredo Moreira-Rosa said:

A side question, i'm really interrested in using the lean part (not the ffi) of lean-zip to implement the Http compression algorithms for LeanIO and so another question would be: would you be willing to provide a lean only version of lean-zip without the ffi as i don't like the idea to add more dependencies than necessary to LeanIO

This is a good question. I should clean this up into an actual reusable library. Currently there's a lot of crap from the development process.

(Another rather esoteric application I have in mind is to implement lean-png, so we have a PNG library, and then once we have a good interval arithmetic library to be able to state a theorem like "This PNG is an accurate graph of the following function". :-)

Gavin Zhao said:

Once the Lean compiler can emit AVX512 instructions (hopefully in a somewhat formally verifiable way) we'd be unstoppable!

The Lean compiler is already very much capable of that if you write enough purely scalar code in a loop.
Could you do the same with rust, using a Rust to Lean tool to verify a rust implementation and optimize?
Also how much was this optimized for a single benchmark? Did the AI know the target benchmark when optimizing?

aggressively optimize using AIs

I was wondering, do you have tips or recommendations on how to do this sort of thing? Or does it mostly consist of general prompts? These are some very impressive results!
